narrative:
The model predicted a 63.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.00 it is only modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so this feature slightly improved the model’s outlook and nudged the prediction toward passing.

Your LSAT score of 25.5 was the third most influential factor. It sits well below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants and therefore pushed the prediction back toward failure, though less forcefully than your third-year class rank.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of weak class standing and a low LSAT outweighed the modest positive signal from your GPA.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your class rank this year, retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, then reapply. These two improvements would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
